Foundations of Persuasive Writing

Before you write a single caption, you need to know what sales copy is for, who you are writing to and what they are struggling with. This module covers the job of copy, how to find your customer's real pain points, how to choose a voice, and the honest psychology that makes people say yes.

**Copywriting** is writing that asks someone to do something: buy, order, send a message, book, register or visit. The words on a WhatsApp status, a flyer, an Instagram caption, a product label or a Facebook ad are all called **copy**. The person who writes them is a **copywriter**. If you sell anything, you are already a copywriter. This course will help you do it on purpose.

General content informs or entertains. Sales copy has a job. A recipe post teaches how to make zobo. A sales post for your zobo tells a busy office worker in Yaba why your chilled zobo will save her afternoon and how to order before 11am. Both can be good writing, but only one is built to produce an order.
A woman writing at a desk
Every seller who writes a status, caption or flyer is doing copywriting, whether she calls it that or not.
The three things every piece of copy needs
**One reader.** Picture one real person, not 'everybody'. Copy written for everybody speaks to nobody.
**One offer.** What exactly are you selling, at what price or package, and what makes it worth it?
**One action.** What should she do next? 'Send me a WhatsApp message with your size' is an action. 'Patronise us' is not.

When copy fails, one of these three is usually missing. Look at the common status message 'Quality bags available. DM for price.' Who is it for? What bag? Why this bag? The only action is to ask for a price, which many people will not bother to do.
Worked example: a bag seller's status, before and after
For example, Ngozi sells ladies' work bags from her shop in Onitsha and posts on WhatsApp status every morning. Her old status gets views but almost no messages.
Before: 'Quality bags available. DM for price. We deliver nationwide.'
She chooses one reader: a young woman starting her first office job who needs one bag that fits a laptop and looks smart.
She chooses one offer: a black faux leather tote that fits a 15-inch laptop, priced at about N18,500 (her current price, which she updates when it changes).
She chooses one action: reply with the word TOTE to reserve one.

After: 'Starting a new job? This black tote fits your 15-inch laptop, charger and lunch pack, and still looks neat in meetings. N18,500. Only 6 left in black. Reply TOTE and I will hold one for you till 6pm today.'

The new status names the reader's situation, gives the real price, shows proof of usefulness (what fits inside) and asks for one easy action. People who reply TOTE have told her they are interested, so she can follow up personally.
The 'so what?' test

Read each sentence you write and ask, as your customer would: **so what?** 'Our hair cream contains shea butter.' So what? 'So your edges stay soft between washes.' Now the sentence matters to her. If you cannot answer 'so what?', the sentence is either missing its benefit or it does not belong. You will use this test throughout the course, and in Module 2 we will go deeper into features and benefits.

Copy is selling in writing

Think of how you sell face to face in the market. You greet the customer, notice what she is looking for, show her the item, answer her worries about price or quality, and then ask, 'Shall I wrap it?' Good copy does the same, except the customer cannot ask you questions. So your words must answer her questions before she asks them: what is it, is it for me, does it work, how much, how do I get it, and can I trust you?

What good copy is not

Good copy is not shouting. Writing everything in capital letters, adding ten emojis or saying 'BEST IN NIGERIA!!!' does not persuade a careful buyer. It is also not lying. A false claim may bring one sale, but it costs you the customer and her friends. The best copy is clear, specific and true, written by someone who understands the buyer's problem.

People do not buy products. They buy a better situation. A mother does not want a blender; she wants to stop grinding pepper on the stone every Saturday. A trader does not want a POS machine; she wants to stop losing customers who have no cash. Your copy works best when it starts with the situation your customer wants to escape or reach.
Three things to know about your customer
**Pain points:** the problems, frustrations or worries she has right now. Example: 'My children's school shoes tear before the term ends.'
**Desires:** what she wants instead. Example: 'Shoes that last the whole term and still look neat on visiting day.'
**Objections:** the reasons she might not buy from you. Example: 'Online sellers send different shoes from the picture.'
A person pointing at a group of customer profiles
Your copy gets sharper when you write for one clear customer instead of a crowd.
Use the customer's own words

The best copy often sounds like something the customer already said. Copywriters call this **voice of customer** research. You do not need a survey company. You already have the material in your phone.
Scroll through your WhatsApp chats with customers from the last three months. Copy every question and complaint into one note.
Read the comments under your posts and under competitors' posts on Instagram, Facebook and TikTok. Note the words people use.
Read reviews of similar products on Jumia or Google Maps listings. Note what people praise and what they complain about.
Ask three loyal customers two questions: 'What made you buy the first time?' and 'What almost stopped you?' Write down their exact words.
Group what you collected into pains, desires and objections.
Respect privacy

Use customers' words to understand them, but do not post their names, numbers or chat screenshots without their clear permission. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 requires a lawful basis, such as consent, for using people's personal data.
Worked example: from chats to a headline
For example, Aisha makes unripe plantain flour in Kaduna and sells 1kg packs. She reads 40 chats from the last two months.
She finds the same questions again and again: 'Will it taste bitter?', 'Is it okay for my father who is diabetic?', 'Is it really plantain or mixed with something?'
Pain point she sees most: people told by a doctor to change their swallow, who miss eating swallow with soup.
Desire in their words: 'I just want to eat swallow without feeling guilty.'

Objections: bitterness, purity, and whether it is safe for a health condition. She notes that she must not make medical claims; she can only describe the ingredient honestly and suggest buyers follow their doctor's advice.
Before: 'Buy our plantain flour, 100% natural.'
After: 'Miss eating swallow? Our unripe plantain flour is made from only dried unripe plantain, nothing added. Smooth, not bitter, and ready in 5 minutes. Ask your doctor how it fits your meal plan.'
The new copy opens with the reader's own feeling ('miss eating swallow'), answers the purity objection directly and handles the health question honestly instead of making a claim she cannot prove.

Turn the pain into an opening line

Once you know the pain point, your first line can name it. A question works well when the answer is obviously yes for the right reader: 'Is your son rough with school shoes?' A statement works too: 'If you bought school shoes twice last term, this is for you.' The reader who has that problem stops scrolling because she feels seen. The reader who does not have it scrolls on, and that is fine.
Do not exaggerate the pain
Naming a real problem is helpful. Inventing fear is manipulation. Avoid lines like 'Your child will be laughed at in school' or false health scares. They damage trust and can break advertising rules.

Update your profile every few months. Customers change, prices change, and new worries appear. When fuel prices rose, for example, many buyers started asking about delivery costs first. A seller who notices that early can address delivery in her copy before anyone asks.

Imagine two food sellers. One writes: 'Dear esteemed customers, kindly be informed that our jollof rice is now available.' The other writes: 'Jollof wey go make you forget your problems is ready. Party flavour, plenty pepper. Order before 1pm.' Both sell jollof. They sound like two different people. That difference is **voice**.
Voice and tone are not the same

**Voice** is your brand's personality. It stays the same across everything you write, the way your friends recognise you on the phone before you say your name. **Tone** is how that voice adjusts to the situation. You speak differently at a wedding and at a condolence visit, but you are still you.
A woman creating posts on her phone and laptop
Your voice is what makes your posts recognisable even before customers see your name.

Choose three words that describe how you want customers to feel about your brand. Then write what each word means in practice, and what it does not mean. This stops your voice drifting from post to post.
Voice word
We do
We don't
Warm
Greet people, thank them, use 'you' and 'we'
Sound cold, use stiff phrases like 'be informed'
Confident
State facts clearly: 'This fabric does not fade'

Playful
Use light humour and the occasional Pidgin line

Worked example: one message, three voices
For example, three different businesses announce that they now deliver to Lekki and Ajah on Saturdays.

A children's clothing brand with a warm, gentle voice: 'Good news for our Lekki and Ajah mums: we now deliver every Saturday. Order by Friday 5pm and your little one's outfit arrives in time for Sunday.'
A streetwear brand with a bold, playful voice: 'Lekki, Ajah, una don dey call us. We hear you. Saturday delivery don land. Order by Friday, wear am Sunday.'
A corporate catering company with a professional voice: 'We now offer Saturday delivery to Lekki and Ajah. Orders confirmed by Friday at 5pm will be delivered between 9am and 1pm on Saturday.'
The facts are identical in all three (areas, day, cut-off time). Only the voice changes, and each one fits its customer. Notice that all three still give the specific details a buyer needs.
Pidgin, local languages or standard English?

Write in the language your customer uses when she is relaxed and buying. Nigerian Pidgin can feel friendly and close for many audiences, especially for food, fashion and entertainment. Yoruba, Hausa, Igbo or other local languages can build strong connection in a local market. Standard English may suit corporate buyers, professional services, health-related products and older customers. Many sellers mix them: a Pidgin hook, then clear English details.
Keep prices, dates, sizes and payment details in clear, simple English or numbers so nobody misreads them.
Only write in a language or style you know well. Badly written Pidgin sounds fake.
Test both: post the same offer in two styles on different days and see which gets more replies. Module 4 shows how to test properly.

Tone for difficult messages

Tone matters most when something goes wrong. If a delivery is late, a joke can feel like you do not care. Use a calm, direct and respectful tone: say what happened, say what you are doing about it, and say what the customer can expect.
Worked example: an apology for late delivery
For example, Blessing runs a cake business in Port Harcourt. Heavy rain delayed three birthday cake deliveries by two hours.
Before: 'Sorry o, rain did us. Cake is coming.'
She removes the casual line, because a birthday is important to the customer.

After: 'I am very sorry. The heavy rain on the East-West Road has delayed our driver. Your cake is safe and packed, and he expects to reach you by 4:30pm. I will send you his location now. As an apology, your next order of small chops is free.'
The customer knows the reason, the new time, how to track the cake and what Blessing is offering to make up for it. Her voice is still warm, but the tone is serious.

Words to avoid in almost every tone: 'kindly be informed', 'we regret any inconvenience this may have caused' and other stiff phrases. They sound like a form letter. Say it the way a respectful person would say it face to face: 'I am sorry your order is late. Here is what I am doing about it.'

The psychology of persuasion: benefits, AIDA and honest influence
Turn product features into benefits using the 'which means' bridge

People decide with feelings and then justify with facts. That does not mean customers are foolish. It means your copy must do two jobs: help her **feel** that the product solves her problem, and give her the **facts** to feel safe saying yes.
Features and benefits

A **feature** is a fact about the product: what it is or has. A **benefit** is what that feature does for the customer. A simple bridge connects them: write the feature, then add '**which means**' and finish the sentence from the customer's point of view.
Feature
Which means (benefit)
Rechargeable fan with 12-hour battery
You can sleep through the night even when NEPA takes light
Adire fabric dyed with fixed colour
It still looks bright after many washes
Meal prep delivered on Sunday
You do not cook after work from Monday to Friday
POS terminal accepts tap-to-pay
Customers who carry no cash can still buy from you

Some features need more than one 'which means' step. 'Stainless steel pot' leads to 'which means it does not rust', which leads to 'which means you buy one pot and use it for years'. Keep going until you reach something the customer truly cares about. Then keep the feature in the copy as proof.
A thinking face emoji
Customers think 'what is in it for me?' Benefits answer that question.
AIDA: a map for any sales message

**AIDA** is one of the oldest models in advertising. It stands for Attention, Interest, Desire and Action. It describes the steps a reader goes through before buying, and it gives you an order to write in.
**Attention:** a first line or image that makes the right person stop. Often it names her problem or a strong benefit.
**Interest:** a few details that make her want to know more. What is it? How is it different?
**Desire:** benefits, proof and a picture of her life with the product.
**Action:** one clear instruction, with any honest reason to act now.
AIDA: from many viewers to a few buyers
Attention: many people notice
Interest: some read on
Desire: fewer want it
Action: buyers respond
Each stage loses some readers, so every line must earn the next one.
Worked example: AIDA for a tailoring service
For example, Halima is a tailor in Kano who sews ready-to-wear kaftans for men and wants more orders before Sallah.
Before: 'We sew kaftans. Contact us.'
Attention: 'Sallah is in 3 weeks. Is your kaftan ready?'
Interest: 'We sew men's kaftans in 5 days from your measurements, using cotton that does not shrink after washing.'
Desire: 'Neat embroidery on the neck and cuffs, sized to fit, so you look sharp at Eid prayers and family visits. See photos of last year's orders in my catalogue.'
Action: 'I can take 15 more orders before Sallah. Send your measurements on WhatsApp today with the word KAFTAN.'
The message follows the reader's thinking from 'this is about me' to 'I want this' to 'I know exactly what to do'. The 15-order limit is honest because Halima can only sew so many in time.
Six principles of influence
Psychologist Robert Cialdini described six principles of influence in his well-known book Influence. Used honestly, they help buyers make decisions. Used dishonestly, they become tricks.
Principle
Honest use in copy
Dishonest use to avoid
Social proof
Share real reviews and photos from real customers
Fake reviews or bought followers
Scarcity
'Only 8 pieces left in this fabric' when true
Saying 'last few' every day for months
Authority
Mention your real training, NAFDAC number or years of experience
Claiming certificates you do not have
Reciprocity
Give a free useful tip, sample or guide
Gifts with hidden conditions
Commitment
Ask a small step first: 'Reply YES for the price list'
Pressuring people after a small yes
Liking
Show your face, your story and your team
Pretending to be someone you are not
Manipulation to avoid
**Fake countdowns:** a 'sale ends tonight' message that you repeat next week with the same offer.
**Shaming:** copy that makes people feel ugly, poor or stupid so they buy. It may work once, but it builds resentment.
**Hidden costs:** showing a low price and adding delivery, packaging or 'service charge' only after payment.
**Pressure after payment questions:** if a buyer asks for time to think, give it. A short follow-up later is fine; ten messages in a day is not.
A simple check before you post: would you be comfortable if the customer later saw exactly how and why you wrote each line? If the answer is yes, your persuasion is honest.
Honesty is also the law

Nigeria's Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC) enforces consumer protection law that forbids false or misleading claims about goods and services. False 'limited time' offers, fake reviews and exaggerated health claims can get you into trouble as well as lose you customers.

Core Copy Formats

Most small business selling happens in four short formats: the headline or first line, the product description, the social media caption and the call to action. This module gives you tested structures for each one, with many before-and-after rewrites from Nigerian businesses.

On a phone, most people see only your first line, the picture and maybe the price before deciding whether to keep reading. On Instagram, a long caption is cut off after the first line or two with a 'more' link. On WhatsApp status, people tap past in a second. So the **headline**, meaning the title or first line, is the most important part of your copy. If it fails, nothing else gets read.

A good headline does one of three things for the right reader: it names her problem, promises a clear benefit, or makes her curious in a way that is relevant to the product. It does not need to be clever. Clear beats clever almost every time.
A person scrolling a social media feed on a phone
Your first line competes with everything else in her feed, so it must speak to her straight away.

The 4 U's check
Copywriters often test headlines with the **4 U's**. A strong headline is usually high on at least two or three of them.
**Useful:** does it promise something the reader values?
**Urgent:** is there a real reason to read or act now (a date, a season, a stock limit)?
**Unique:** does it say something your competitors are not saying?
**Ultra-specific:** does it include details such as numbers, places, times or sizes?

Useful to the reader
Urgent for a real reason
Unique to your business
Ultra-specific with details
Score each headline on these four; rewrite any that scores on only one.
Worked example: improving a laundry service headline
For example, Chioma runs a laundry and ironing service in Enugu for working people and students.
Before: 'Best Laundry Services in Town.' Useful? Vaguely. Urgent? No. Unique? No, every laundry says this. Specific? No.
She adds a specific benefit: 'Your clothes washed, ironed and delivered in 48 hours.'
She adds the place and who it is for: 'Busy in Enugu? Your clothes washed, ironed and delivered in 48 hours.'
She adds an honest urgency for the season: 'Resumption week: drop off by Thursday, wear crisp uniforms on Monday.'
She now has two strong options to test on different days.
The new headlines score on useful, specific and, in one case, urgent. They tell the reader exactly what she gets and when, which 'Best Laundry Services in Town' never did.
Write ten, choose one

Professional copywriters rarely use their first headline. They write many and choose. Try this: set a timer for ten minutes and write ten headlines for the same product, using at least four different patterns from the table. Then cross out any that are vague, any you could not prove, and any that sound like every other seller. Read the last two or three aloud and pick the one that sounds most like a helpful friend.
Worked example: ten headlines for solar lanterns
For example, Kemi sells rechargeable solar lanterns in Ibadan. Her old first line was 'Solar lanterns now available.'
How-to: 'How to light your shop all evening without buying fuel.'
Question: 'Tired of buying candles every time light goes?'
Number: '3 reasons traders in Bodija market are switching to solar lanterns.' (She only uses this if it is true that her Bodija customers are doing so.)
Direct benefit: 'Charge it in the sun by day, light your stall by night.'
News: 'New stock: solar lanterns with a phone charging port.'
She crosses out the vague ones and picks 'Charge it in the sun by day, light your stall by night' for her market trader customers.
The chosen headline is simple, specific and shows the benefit in one picture. She keeps the question version to test later on her status.
Avoid clickbait
A headline that promises something the post does not deliver, such as 'You won't believe this price' followed by a normal price, makes people feel tricked. They stop trusting your next post.

Keep the headline short enough to read in one glance on a phone, and let a second line, the **subheadline**, carry supporting detail. For example: headline 'Light your stall all evening without fuel', subheadline 'Solar lantern with phone charging port, about N12,000, delivered in Ibadan.' The headline earns attention; the subheadline earns trust.
Use numbers as digits
On small screens, '48 hours', 'N5,000' and '3 sizes' stand out more than 'forty-eight hours' or 'three sizes'. Digits catch the eye in a scroll.

A product description replaces you, the seller, when the customer cannot touch the product. In a shop she can feel the fabric, smell the cream and check the size. Online, your words and photos must do all of that. A weak description lists a few facts. A strong one helps her picture using the product and answers her doubts.
Features versus benefits, again and deeper

In Module 1 you learnt the 'which means' bridge. In product descriptions you need both sides: **benefits** to create desire and **features** to prove the benefits are real. Lead with the benefit, then support it with the feature.
Features prove, benefits sell

Lead with the benefit on the right, then use the feature on the left as proof.
A four-part structure
**Hook line:** the main benefit for the main customer. 'A work dress that keeps you cool from morning meeting to evening traffic.'
**Benefits with proof:** two to four short lines, each a benefit linked to a feature.
**Practical details:** size, colour options, weight or quantity, ingredients or materials, care instructions, registration numbers where required, delivery time and price.
**Call to action:** how to order or what to send. 'Reply with your size and delivery area.'

Worked example: a shea body butter, before and after
For example, Amaka makes whipped shea body butter in Abuja and sells 250g jars. Her catalogue description was very short.
Before: 'Organic shea butter. Very good for skin. N4,500.'
Problems: 'organic' is a claim she cannot prove without certification; 'very good for skin' is vague; there are no details.
Hook: 'Soft, whipped shea butter that melts into dry skin without leaving you oily.'
Benefits with proof: 'Made with raw unrefined shea butter and coconut oil, so it absorbs quickly. Lightly scented with lemongrass. Whipped for 20 minutes so it spreads easily, even in harmattan.'
Details: '250g glass jar. Ingredients: shea butter, coconut oil, lemongrass essential oil. Store away from direct sun. Price: N4,500 (current price). Delivery within Abuja in 1 to 2 days.'
Action: 'Reply SHEA with your area to order.'

The new description removes the unprovable 'organic' claim, lists the real ingredients, explains why the texture is good and tells the buyer exactly how to order. If she sells a cosmetic widely, she also checks NAFDAC registration requirements and adds her number once she has it.
Use sensory and specific words

Help the buyer feel the product through her screen. Instead of 'nice', say what makes it nice: 'crunchy', 'buttery', 'soft like cotton wool', 'deep wine colour', 'smells like fresh lemongrass'. Instead of 'big', give a measurement or comparison: '45cm wide, fits a 15-inch laptop', 'feeds 4 adults'. Specific words build trust because they sound like someone who has really used the product.

Adapt for each platform
**WhatsApp Business catalogue:** each item has a name, price, description and link. Put the hook and key details first, because people read on a small screen.
**Instagram post:** the hook goes in the first line of the caption; details can follow after line breaks.

**Online marketplace such as Jumia or your own Paystack or Selar store page:** buyers compare many listings, so put the most searched words (product type, size, colour) in the title and use bullet points for details.
Claims that need care

Do not claim a product cures, treats or prevents a disease unless it is approved for that purpose. Food, drinks, cosmetics and herbal products sold widely in Nigeria generally need NAFDAC registration, and health claims are closely controlled. Describe ingredients and use honestly instead.
Worked example: one description, three lengths
For example, Zainab sells a 1.5-litre electric kettle in Kano and needs a short, medium and long version of the same description. She checks every feature on the box before writing.
Short (WhatsApp status, under 20 words): 'Hot water for tea without lighting the stove. 1.5-litre kettle, switches itself off. About N15,000. Reply KETTLE.'
Medium (WhatsApp catalogue): add the features that prove the benefits, taken from the box: stainless steel body, automatic switch-off when the water boils, and the warranty her shop actually offers.
Long (online store page): add the practical details: 1.5 litres, 220 to 240V, cable length, what is in the box, how to clean it, delivery areas and return policy.
She keeps the same hook in all three so the product is recognised wherever a buyer sees it.
Each platform gets the length it suits, but the core benefit and the facts never change, so the seller never contradicts herself.
Finally, update descriptions when something changes. If the price goes up or a colour sells out, change the listing the same day. An out-of-date description causes arguments and refunds.

Worked example: a one-day status series for a small chops business
For example, Tolu sells small chops packs in Ibadan for parties and office events. Her old habit was to post one flyer with 12 items and the words 'Order now'.
Status 1 (morning, photo of a packed tray): 'Planning a birthday or office party this weekend? 50 small chops packs ready in 24 hours.'
Status 2 (video of puff-puff being fried): 'Fresh, not reheated. We fry on the morning of your event.'
Status 3 (photo of the pack opened): 'Each pack: 4 puff-puff, 2 samosas, 2 spring rolls, 1 peppered chicken wing. About N2,000 per pack this month.'
Status 4 (screenshot of a customer message, shared with permission): 'Thank you, the guests finished everything!'
Status 5 (evening): 'I can take 3 more weekend orders. Reply PACK with the date and number of guests.'

Instead of one crowded flyer, the series gives attention, proof of freshness, clear contents and price, social proof, and an honest limit with a simple action. Each status can stand alone, but together they follow the AIDA order.

Writing Instagram captions

Then give value: a tip, a short story, how the product is made, or how to use it. Add proof or details, then one call to action. Short paragraphs with line breaks are easier to read on a phone than one long block.

For example, Bisi sells hand-dyed adire fabric in Abeokuta and wants to reach buyers outside Ogun State.

Proof and details: 'Cotton, 2 yards per piece, about N8,000 each. Wash in cold water with mild soap to keep the colour rich. Shipping across Nigeria.'

**Pidgin and local languages:** a Pidgin or Yoruba hook can feel warm; keep price, size and ordering steps in clear words.

A **call to action** (CTA) is the part of your copy that tells the reader exactly what to do next. It may be a sentence, a button or a link. Many good posts fail at this last step: the reader is interested, but the next step is unclear, slow or risky, so she does nothing.
What makes a strong call to action
**A clear action verb:** reply, send, book, tap, order, call, pay, register.
**One action, not five:** 'Call, DM, WhatsApp or visit our website' makes people hesitate. Choose the channel you respond to fastest.
**The exact next step:** what to send or where to tap. 'Reply with your size and area' is better than 'Contact us'.
**Low effort:** the fewer steps, the better. A word to reply with is easier than a form.
**A reason to act now, if it is true:** a deadline, limited stock or a delivery cut-off.

Strong call to action

Remove friction

**Friction** is anything that makes the next step harder. Common friction points for Nigerian online buyers include not knowing the full price with delivery, not knowing how to pay, worrying about being scammed and waiting a long time for a reply. Your CTA and the text around it should remove as many of these as you can.
State the price and the delivery cost (or how it is calculated) before the CTA.
Say how payment works: transfer to a business account in your registered business name, a Paystack or Flutterwave payment link, a Moniepoint or Opay POS on delivery, or pay on delivery in some areas.
Add reassurance: your response time, return or exchange policy, or delivery tracking.
Make the channel one tap: a WhatsApp link, a 'Send message' button or a payment link.
Create a WhatsApp click-to-chat link

WhatsApp offers a free **click-to-chat** link. When someone taps it, a chat with you opens, even if they have not saved your number. You can add a pre-filled message so the customer only needs to press send. The format is https://wa.me/ followed by your full number in international format with no plus sign, zeros or dashes. To pre-fill text, add ?text= and your message, with spaces written as %20.
Worked example: building a click-to-chat link
For example, Grace sells grocery packs in Abuja. Her WhatsApp number is 0803 123 4567 (an illustrative number) and she wants the customer's first message to say 'Hello, I want a grocery pack'.
Remove the first 0 and add Nigeria's country code 234: 2348031234567.
Start the link: https://wa.me/2348031234567
Add the message, replacing spaces with %20: ?text=Hello%2C%20I%20want%20a%20grocery%20pack (the comma becomes %2C).
Full link: https://wa.me/2348031234567?text=Hello%2C%20I%20want%20a%20grocery%20pack
She tests the link on her own phone before sharing it, then adds it to her Instagram bio and Facebook posts with the CTA 'Tap to order your pack on WhatsApp'.
Customers who tap the link land in a chat with the message already typed. Grace instantly knows what they want, and buyers do not need to save her number first.
Call to action checklist
One clear action verb
Exact next step stated
Price and delivery shown
Payment method explained
Honest reason to act now
Check every CTA against this list before you post.
Protect your buyers and yourself

Ask customers to pay only into an account in your business or registered name, and never ask for card PINs, OTPs or passwords. Saying this in your copy reassures buyers who fear scams, and it protects you from impostors using your name.
Where to place the call to action

Put the main CTA at the end of your message, after the reader has the information she needs. In longer posts, product pages and emails, repeat the same CTA once near the top for people who are already convinced. On a picture flyer, the CTA and phone number should be big enough to read on a small phone screen without zooming. Never hide the ordering details in a comment or ask people to 'check the link in my bio' without saying what they will find there.

Finally, be ready for the response. A strong CTA that leads to a two-day wait for a reply wastes the sale. Use WhatsApp Business quick replies and greeting messages so customers get an instant first answer, and set aside times each day to respond fully.

PAS: Problem, Agitate, Solution
**PAS** is a short framework that works well for ads because it starts where the reader is: with a problem.
**Problem:** name a specific problem your reader recognises.
**Agitate:** describe what that problem costs her: time, money, stress, embarrassment. Be honest and specific, not dramatic.
**Solution:** present your product as the way out, with proof and a call to action.
PAS framework
Problem: name it
Agitate: show the cost
Solution: your offer
Action: one next step
PAS moves the reader from a problem she feels to a clear way out.
Worked example: PAS ad for a generator servicing business
For example, Uche runs a small generator repair and servicing workshop in Owerri and wants to run a click-to-WhatsApp ad to homeowners within his area.
Before: 'We repair all kinds of generators. Call us today.'
Problem: 'Does your generator start, run for a few minutes, then go off?'

Agitate: 'You keep pulling the rope, food in the freezer starts to spoil and you end up buying fuel for a machine that will not stay on. Small faults like a dirty carburettor or a worn plug often get worse when ignored.'
Solution: 'We service petrol generators at your home in Owerri: carburettor cleaning, plug and oil change, and a full test run. Service from about N10,000 depending on the size of the generator.'
Action and button: 'Tap Send WhatsApp message and tell us your generator brand and size.'
Headline under the image: 'Home generator servicing in Owerri'

The ad speaks to a frustration the right reader feels strongly, explains the real cost of ignoring it, then offers a specific service with a starting price and a one-tap action. The agitation is factual, not frightening.
PAS or AIDA?

Use **PAS** when your product solves a clear, felt problem: repairs, pest control, hair loss products within legal claims, school fees savings plans, delivery services. Use **AIDA** when the product is more about desire than pain: fashion, cakes, décor, gifts, travel. Many good ads mix them, opening with a problem and then building desire.
Rules to respect

Meta reviews ads before they run and can reject them. Its Advertising Standards do not allow ads that assert or imply someone's personal attributes, such as health conditions, financial status or body shape. That changes how you write the Problem step.
Likely to be rejected
Better wording
Are you fat? Lose belly fat fast!
Comfortable activewear for your morning walks
Are you broke? Make money now!
Learn bead-making as a skill you can sell
Do you have diabetes?
Unripe plantain flour: just dried unripe plantain, nothing added
Talk about the situation, not the person

'Does your generator keep going off?' is about the generator. 'Are you poor?' is about the person. Describe situations and products, not people's bodies, health or money. Advertising in mainstream Nigerian media is also regulated by ARCON, the Advertising Regulatory Council of Nigeria, so check its rules if you grow into radio, TV or billboards.
Keep the primary text easy to scan

Only the first part of the primary text shows before a 'See more' link, so put the problem or main benefit in the opening line. Use short lines and one idea per line. Make the image do part of the work: a photo of the product being used by someone like your customer usually says more than text printed on the picture. If you include a price, make sure it matches what people will be charged when they message you.

Finally, write the ad to match where people land. If the button opens WhatsApp, have a greeting message ready. If it opens a page, the page headline should repeat the ad's promise so people know they are in the right place.

A **landing page** is a single web page built for one purpose: to get visitors to take one action, such as buying, registering or sending a message. A **sales page** is a longer landing page that sells a product or course. You need one when your offer needs more explanation than a caption allows, for example a training programme, a bulk catering package or a pre-order.
Unlike a full website with many menus, a landing page removes distractions. Every section leads to the same button.

**Proof:** real testimonials, photos of past work, numbers you can back up, your experience or registration.

Call to action button: 'Reserve my seat' linking to a Paystack payment page.

Writing the FAQ section

The FAQ is where you handle objections calmly. Take the questions straight from your chats. Answer each in one to three sentences, and never dodge. If the honest answer is 'No, you need an oven at home to practise', say so and suggest what she can do instead. A direct answer to an uncomfortable question builds more trust than a page that pretends there are no downsides. Keep the most common question, often about price, payment in parts or refunds, at the top.

Before you share the page, read it as a stranger would. Could someone who has never heard of you understand the offer, believe it, and pay without asking a single question? If not, the missing answer belongs on the page.

A **broadcast list** in WhatsApp lets you send one message to many contacts at once. Each person receives it as a private message from you, and their reply comes back to you privately. Nobody sees who else is on the list. This makes broadcasts feel personal, which is why they are powerful, and also why badly written ones feel like spam.
How broadcast lists work
Only contacts who have **saved your number** in their phone receive your broadcast. If someone has not saved you, the message will not reach them.
Each list has a limit on the number of contacts (it has long been 256 per list; check the current limit in your app).
You can create several lists, for example 'Wholesale buyers', 'Lagos retail' and 'Abuja retail'.
In the WhatsApp Business app you can also use **labels** to group chats, **quick replies** for common answers, a **catalogue** for your products, and greeting and away messages.
Businesses that need to message very large numbers of people use the WhatsApp Business Platform through an approved provider, which has its own rules on opt-in and message templates.
A person sending a message from a phone
A broadcast arrives like a personal message, so it should read like one.
Permission first

Ask before you add someone to a broadcast list, and make it easy to leave. This is good manners, it keeps people from blocking or reporting you, and it respects Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023, which expects a lawful basis such as consent when you use people's contact details for marketing.
Worked example: asking permission
For example, Ifeoma sells wholesale and retail fabrics in Aba. After every sale she wants to invite buyers to her new-stock list.
Before: she added every customer's number to a broadcast list without asking. Some replied 'Who is this?' and some blocked her.

After a sale, she now sends: 'Thank you for your order, Chika. I send new fabric arrivals about once a week, with prices. Would you like to receive them? Reply YES to join, and you can reply STOP any time.'
She saves the customer's number, adds those who reply YES to the right list and labels them in WhatsApp Business.
She reminds new subscribers to save her number so the broadcasts reach them.
Her list is smaller but everyone on it wants her messages, so more people open and reply. Very few people block her.
Structure of a good broadcast
**Personal opening:** a short greeting. Avoid 'Dear valued customer'.
**One main point:** new stock, a restock, an offer, a reminder or a useful tip. Not all of them at once.
**Key details:** price, sizes, quantities, deadline.
**One simple action:** a word to reply with, or a link.
**Easy exit:** occasionally remind people they can reply STOP.
Worked example: a restock broadcast, before and after
For example, Ifeoma has just restocked a popular lace that sold out last month.
Before: 'DEAR VALUED CUSTOMERS!!! NEW GOODS HAVE ARRIVED!!! ALL KINDS OF LACE, ANKARA, GEORGE, ASO OKE. COME AND BUY. PRICES ARE VERY CHEAP!!!'

After: 'Good morning. The wine Swiss lace that sold out last month is back. 5 yards for about N38,000. I have 14 pieces, and 6 are already reserved. Reply WINE to reserve one. Photos and close-up video below.'
She follows with one short video showing the lace in daylight.
The new message is calm, specific and personal, with real stock numbers and one action. The capital letters and vague 'all kinds' list are gone.

Send useful message

Each broadcast should teach you something that makes the next one better.
How often to send

There is no single correct number. Many small sellers find that one to two broadcasts a week, sent at a time customers are free, works better than daily messages. Watch the signs: if replies drop or people ask to leave, you are sending too often or the messages are not useful. Mix sales messages with helpful ones, such as how to care for a fabric or what to wear to an owambe this season.

Scammers sometimes copy a seller's name and photo. Tell your list which account number you use and that you will never ask for card PINs or OTPs. Send payment details only after a customer has confirmed an order with you.

Email may feel old-fashioned next to WhatsApp, but it is still important for businesses that sell to professionals, organisations, diaspora customers and people who buy online courses or services. You own your email list, unlike your followers on a social platform. If an account is restricted, your email list still works.
Three things people see before they open
**Sender name:** use a real name people recognise, for example 'Amaka from Shea by Amaka', rather than 'info' or 'noreply'.
**Subject line:** the headline of your email. Short, specific and honest.

**Preview text:** the line that shows after the subject in many inboxes. If you do not set it, the inbox shows the first words of your email, which may be 'View in browser'. Most email tools let you write it.

In email, the sender name, subject line and preview text decide whether the rest is read.

One email, one goal

Each sales email should have one goal: to get a click to the sales page, a reply, a booking or a payment. Write it like a letter to one person. Short paragraphs, a friendly opening, the main message, and one button or link repeated at most twice. A **P.S.** at the end is often read, so use it to repeat the deadline or main benefit.
Worked example: a launch email for a catering package
For example, Ruth runs a catering business in Abuja and is launching office lunch packages for companies with 10 or more staff.
Before: subject 'Ruth's Kitchen Update', body a long list of every dish she makes, with no price and no clear next step.
Subject: 'Hot office lunches for your team, delivered by 12:30'
Preview text: 'Weekly packages for teams of 10 or more in Abuja.'
Opening: 'Hello Tunde, many office managers tell me lunch orders take up their whole morning.'

Main message: 'Our weekly lunch package delivers hot meals to your office every working day by 12:30pm. Your staff choose from 3 meals a day by WhatsApp, and you get one invoice at the end of the week.'
Offer: 'Packages from about N3,500 per person per day for teams of 10 or more (current pricing). The first day is a free tasting for up to 10 people.'
Call to action: a button 'Book a free tasting day' and a P.S.: 'Tasting days for October are limited to 8 companies, because we deliver everything ourselves.'
The email is addressed to one person's problem, explains how the service works, gives a starting price and a low-risk first step, and closes with an honest limit.
A simple three-email sequence
Three-email launch sequence
Day 1: announce and explain
Day 3: proof and FAQ
Last day: honest reminder
A short sequence gives busy readers more than one chance to act, without flooding their inbox.
**Email 1, announcement:** what it is, who it is for, the main benefit and the deadline.
**Email 2, proof and questions:** a customer story, photos and answers to the top three objections.
**Email 3, reminder:** short, friendly reminder that the offer or registration closes today.
Consent and unsubscribe

Only email people who agreed to hear from you, for example by ticking a box on your sign-up form or asking to join. Never buy email lists. Every marketing email should include a clear unsubscribe link, which email tools such as Mailchimp, Brevo and MailerLite add automatically. Large inbox providers like Gmail and Yahoo now expect bulk senders to make unsubscribing easy, and emails that people mark as spam reduce the chance your future emails reach anyone's inbox.
Make the email easy to read on a phone
Keep paragraphs to two or three short sentences.
Use one simple layout. A plain, letter-style email often feels more personal than a heavily designed one.
Make the button big and the button text specific: 'Book a free tasting day' rather than 'Click here'.
Add your business name, address or phone number at the bottom so readers know who you are.
Send a test to yourself and read it on your phone before sending to your list.

After sending, look at three numbers in your email tool: how many people opened, how many clicked the link and how many unsubscribed. Opens tell you about the subject line, clicks tell you about the body and the call to action, and a jump in unsubscribes tells you the email was not welcome.
Start small

Several email tools offer free plans for small lists; check each tool's current limits. Start by collecting emails from customers who buy online or attend your classes, with their permission, and send one genuinely useful email a month.

Storytelling in sales copy: before, after and the bridge
Explain why stories make sales copy more believable

People remember stories more easily than lists of features. A story lets the reader see someone like herself facing a problem and finding a way through. It also carries proof in a natural way: instead of saying 'our tutoring works', you show one child's journey from struggling to confident.

In sales copy, the customer is the hero of the story, not your business. Your product is the helper or tool that makes the change possible. When sellers make themselves the hero ('We are the best, we have won awards'), readers lose interest. When the reader sees herself in the hero, she leans in.
A woman writing a story in a notebook
A short, true story often persuades more than a long list of features.
Before, After, Bridge (BAB)
**Before:** the situation and frustration before the product.
**After:** what life looks like once the problem is solved.
**Bridge:** how the product or service got her from before to after, and how the reader can do the same.
Before, After, Bridge
Before: the struggle
After: the better situation
Bridge: how she got there
Show the contrast first, then reveal the bridge that connects the two.
Worked example: a BAB story for a home tutoring service
For example, Esther runs after-school maths tutoring in Benin City. A parent agreed that his daughter's story could be shared using her first name.
Before: 'In January, Osaro dreaded maths homework. She would sit at the table for an hour and finish two questions, and her mum had to beg her to try.'
After: 'By the end of the term, she was finishing her homework before dinner and asked for extra fractions practice.'
Bridge: 'What changed? Two evenings a week, we went back to the basics she had missed, used objects and drawings for fractions, and gave her small wins every session.'
Call to action: 'We have 4 places left for this term in GRA and Ugbowo. Reply MATHS and I will tell you how the first free assessment works.'

The story shows a believable change with specific details (two questions in an hour, fractions, two evenings a week) instead of claiming 'excellent results'. It ends with a clear, low-risk next step. It does not promise that every child will improve in the same way.

Compare 'Our customers love our cakes' with 'Last Saturday, a mother in Ikorodu sent me a voice note at 11pm saying the children had eaten the cake before the photos were taken.' The second feels real because it includes a day, a place, a person and a small surprising detail. Use details you actually know. If you do not remember them, ask the customer, or tell a smaller story you do know well.
Worked example: a founder story for a pap business
For example, Nkechi makes and sells fermented pap (ogi) in Enugu in hygienic packs.
Before: 'We are the best pap producer in Enugu. Our pap is very hygienic. Order now.'

She rewrites it as a founder story: 'When my first child started eating solid food, I wanted pap I could trust. I watched how my mother soaked, ground and sieved the corn, and I learnt to do it in a clean kitchen with filtered water.'
She adds the bridge to the customer: 'Today I make the same pap for other mothers, sealed in 1kg packs, so you get the taste of home-made ogi without the soaking and sieving.'
She adds proof and action: 'See how we make it in the video. Reply OGI to order for delivery in Enugu.'

The story replaces empty claims ('best', 'very hygienic') with a believable reason she cares about cleanliness and a picture of how it is made. Note that she does not claim health benefits she cannot prove.
Never invent a story
A made-up customer story is a fake testimonial, even if it sounds realistic. Use real stories with permission, change or remove names if the customer prefers, and never exaggerate results.

Keep stories short in captions and statuses: three to five sentences is often enough. Save longer stories for landing pages, emails and video. You can also tell a story across several WhatsApp statuses in one day, one stage per status.

An **objection** is a reason a customer hesitates. In face-to-face selling, she tells you and you answer. Online, she simply scrolls away. Good copy answers the main objections in advance, so the buyer's doubts are settled before she leaves.
Common objections and how copy answers them

What she is thinking
How your copy can answer
Trust
Will I pay and receive nothing?
Business name and address, real reviews, account in business name, pay on delivery option where possible
What I ordered vs what I got

Real photos and videos in daylight, measurements, exchange policy

Show value: cost per use, what is included, quality details; offer a smaller size

Real words from real customers answer the trust objection better than any claim you make about yourself.
Worked example: answering the price objection
For example, Sade sells handmade leather sandals in Ibadan at about N25,000 a pair. Many people reply 'too expensive'.
Before: 'Original leather sandals. N25,000. No price negotiation.'
She breaks down the value: 'Full cow leather upper and a stitched sole, not glued, so it does not peel after rainy season.'

She shows cost over time: 'If a pair lasts you two years of regular wear, that is about N1,050 a month.' She only says this because her past customers report this kind of wear; otherwise she would leave it out.
She addresses fit: 'Send your foot length in cm and I will confirm your size before you pay.'
She offers an option: 'Prefer something lighter on the pocket? Our slip-on style is about N15,000.'
Instead of arguing about price, the copy explains why the sandals cost what they cost, reduces the risk of the wrong size and offers a cheaper choice. Some buyers will still say no, and that is fine.
Testimonials: powerful and easy to misuse

A **testimonial** is a customer's own words about your product. It is one of the strongest forms of social proof because it comes from someone who is not the seller. That is exactly why fake or misleading testimonials are so damaging, and why consumer protection rules in many countries treat them seriously. In Nigeria, the FCCPC enforces law against misleading representations to consumers.
Ethical versus unethical testimonials
Ethical
Unethical
Real customer, real words
Permission to share
Gift or discount disclosed
Typical results shown
Invented or paid reviews
Screenshots shared without asking
Hidden free products
Rare best result as normal
If a testimonial would mislead a reasonable buyer, do not use it.
**Ask for permission** in writing, for example on WhatsApp: 'May I share your message on my status, with your first name only?'
**Keep their meaning.** You may shorten a testimonial or fix a spelling mistake, but do not change what they said or add claims.
**Hide private details** such as phone numbers, profile photos and other chats in any screenshot.
**Disclose connections.** If you gave someone a free product or payment for a review, say so, for example 'received a free sample'.
**Do not present unusual results as typical,** especially for skin, hair, weight or income products.
**Never write reviews yourself** or ask friends to post reviews for products they have not used.
Guarantees and policies you can keep

A clear policy removes risk for the buyer: 'Exchange within 3 days if the size is wrong, item unused and with tags.' Only promise what you can afford to honour. A generous policy you break is worse than a modest one you keep. Write the conditions plainly so there is no argument later.
Worked example: turning a messy screenshot into an ethical testimonial

For example, Sade receives this WhatsApp message from a customer named Yetunde: 'Omo these sandals are sweet!! Wore them to my cousin's wedding and danced all night, no pain. My sister wants one too, abeg send price.'
She asks: 'Thank you, Yetunde! May I share your message on my status and page, with your first name only?' Yetunde replies 'Yes, no problem.'
She keeps Yetunde's words and meaning but removes the line asking for a price, which is not part of the review.
In the screenshot, she covers the phone number and profile photo.
Final testimonial: 'Wore them to my cousin's wedding and danced all night, no pain.' Yetunde, Ibadan.
She saves the permission message in a 'Testimonials' label in WhatsApp Business in case anyone asks.

The testimonial is real, specific, shared with permission and free of private details. It answers the comfort objection in a customer's own voice, which is more believable than Sade saying 'very comfortable'.
Who it is not for
Saying who your product is not for builds trust. 'These sandals are not for wide feet; try our slip-on style instead' tells the buyer you care about the right fit, not just a sale.

Good copy is rarely written; it is rewritten. Your first draft gets the ideas down. Editing makes it clear, short and persuasive. Testing then shows you which version your customers actually prefer, so you stop guessing.
A seven-point editing checklist
**Reader:** is it clearly written for one type of customer?
**First line:** would she stop scrolling for it?
**Benefits:** does every feature have a 'which means'?
**Specifics:** have you replaced vague words with numbers, places and details?
**Proof:** is there at least one reason to believe you?
**Action:** is there one clear call to action with the exact next step?
**Truth:** is every claim true and can you prove it?
Two versions of a design being compared side by side
A/B testing compares two versions so your customers' responses, not your guesses, decide.
Cut, simplify, read aloud
Cut filler words: 'very', 'really', 'in order to', 'we wish to inform you that'.
Use short words: 'use' not 'utilise', 'buy' not 'purchase', 'help' not 'facilitate'.
Keep most sentences short. One idea per sentence.
Read your copy aloud. Wherever you stumble or run out of breath, rewrite.
Free tools such as the Hemingway Editor highlight long, hard sentences.
Worked example: editing a caption
For example, Hauwa sells home-made zobo drinks in Jos and wrote this first draft.

Draft (52 words): 'We wish to inform our esteemed customers that we are now in the business of producing very high quality and really refreshing zobo drinks that are made with the best ingredients in order to satisfy your thirst. Kindly contact us for more information about prices and delivery. Thank you.'
She cuts filler ('we wish to inform', 'very', 'really', 'in order to') and vague words ('best ingredients').
She adds specifics: ingredients, size, price, delivery time.

Final (36 words): 'Chilled zobo made with hibiscus, ginger and pineapple, no artificial colour. 50cl bottles, about N700 each or N8,000 for 12. Delivered cold in Jos by 1pm. Reply ZOBO with how many you want.'
The edited version is shorter but says much more: what it is made of, the size, the price, the delivery time and exactly how to order.
A/B testing: let customers decide

An **A/B test** compares two versions of the same copy, version A and version B, that differ in only **one thing**, such as the headline or the call to action. You show both to similar audiences and measure which gets a better result. If you change many things at once, you will not know which change made the difference.
The A/B testing cycle
Pick one thing to test
Write versions A and B
Show both fairly
Measure one result
Keep the winner
Each round teaches you one thing about your customers; then you test the next thing.
Worked example: testing two status headlines
For example, Hauwa wants to know whether a price-led or a taste-led first line gets more zobo orders on her WhatsApp status.
Thing to test: the first line only. Picture, price, CTA and posting time stay the same.
Version A: 'Chilled zobo, 12 bottles for about N8,000.'
Version B: 'Hibiscus, ginger and pineapple, served ice cold.'
She posts A on Monday and Wednesday, and B on Tuesday and Thursday, at 10am each day, for two weeks.
She records views and ZOBO replies in a simple sheet: A got 410 views and 21 replies in total; B got 395 views and 9 replies.
Reply rate: A is 21 out of 410, about 5.1%; B is 9 out of 395, about 2.3%.
The price-led headline got more than twice the reply rate in her test, so she keeps it and next tests the call to action. She remembers that one small test is a clue, not a law, and re-tests later.

Persuasive writing: one reader, one offer, one action.
This is the video for module 1 of Copywriting for Sales.
Why it matters
If you sell, you are a copywriter
Copy asks someone to take an action
Know your customer's pain and desire
Choose a voice and the right tone
Persuade honestly, never with tricks
Copywriting is writing that asks someone to do something: buy, order, book or message. If you sell anything, you are already a copywriter.
Good copy starts with your customer's problem, in her own words.
It sounds like you, and changes tone for the moment.
And it persuades honestly.
Worked example
Ngozi's bag status, before and after
Before
Quality bags available
DM for price
We deliver nationwide
After
Starting a new job?
Black tote fits your 15-inch laptop
N18,500. Only 6 left in black
Reply TOTE, held till 6pm today
For example, Ngozi sells work bags in Onitsha. Her status said, quality bags available, DM for price. Who is it for? What bag? Why this one? It got views, but almost no messages.
She chose one reader: a young woman starting her first office job. One offer: a black tote that fits a 15-inch laptop, about 18,500 naira. One action: reply TOTE and she will hold one till 6pm.
Now the reader sees her own situation, the real price, and one easy thing to do.
Know your customer
Pain points, desires, objections
Pain point: the problem she has now
Desire: what she wants instead
Objection: why she might not buy
Collect her real words from your chats
Open with her words about her problem
People do not buy products. They buy a better situation. A pain point is her problem now: my children's school shoes tear before the term ends.
A desire is what she wants instead: shoes that last the whole term.
An objection is why she might not buy: online sellers send different shoes from the picture.
You already have this research in your phone. Copy questions and complaints from your chats, comments and reviews. Do not post customers' names or chat screenshots without permission.
Then open with her words. Is your son rough with school shoes? The right reader stops, because she feels seen.
Aisha's plantain flour headline
Never make medical claims you cannot prove.
Reads 40 chats from two months
Pain: told to change swallow, misses it
Objections: bitter? pure? safe?
Opens with: Miss eating swallow?
For example, Aisha makes unripe plantain flour in Kaduna. She reads 40 customer chats from the last two months.
The pain she sees most: people told by a doctor to change their swallow, who miss eating it with soup.
The objections: will it taste bitter, is it really pure, and is it safe for a health condition?
Her new copy opens: Miss eating swallow? Only dried unripe plantain, nothing added. Smooth, not bitter, ready in 5 minutes.
And it ends: ask your doctor how it fits your meal plan. She handles the health question honestly, instead of making a claim she cannot prove.
Voice and tone
Same voice, different tone
Promotion
Light and warm
Pidgin hook is fine
Clear price and cut-off time
Apology
Calm, direct, respectful
What happened, the new time
What you will do about it

Voice is your brand's personality. It stays the same. Tone adjusts to the moment, the way you speak differently at a wedding and a condolence visit. For a promotion, a playful Pidgin hook can work, but keep prices and dates in clear words.

When something goes wrong, be serious. For example, Blessing's cakes in Port Harcourt were delayed by heavy rain. Not, sorry o, rain did us. Instead: I am very sorry, the rain delayed our driver, your cake is safe, and he will reach you by 4:30pm.
Step by step
AIDA: Halima's kaftan message
Use 'which means' to turn every feature into a benefit.
Attention: Sallah is in 3 weeks
Interest: kaftans sewn in 5 days
Desire: neat embroidery, sized to fit
Action: send measurements, word KAFTAN
AIDA stands for Attention, Interest, Desire and Action. For example, Halima, a tailor in Kano. Attention: Sallah is in 3 weeks. Is your kaftan ready?
Interest: we sew men's kaftans in 5 days, using cotton that does not shrink.
Desire: neat embroidery, sized to fit, so you look sharp at Eid prayers. See last year's orders in my catalogue.
Action: I can take 15 more orders before Sallah. Send your measurements on WhatsApp today. That limit is honest, because she can only sew so many in time.
A feature is a fact. A benefit is what it does for her. Rechargeable fan with a 12-hour battery, which means you sleep through the night when there is no light.
Honest influence
Persuade, never manipulate
Honest
Real reviews from real customers
Only 8 left, when true
Your real training or NAFDAC number
Dishonest
Fake reviews, bought followers
Last few, every day for months
Hidden delivery costs
Social proof, scarcity and authority help buyers decide, when they are true. Share real reviews, a true stock limit, and your real experience.
Fake reviews, fake countdowns, shaming and hidden costs destroy trust. And Nigeria's consumer protection law, enforced by the FCCPC, forbids false or misleading claims.
Ask yourself: would I be comfortable if the customer saw exactly why I wrote each line?
Key points
Remember
One reader, one offer, one action
Ask 'so what?' of every sentence
Start with her pain, in her words
Steady voice; tone fits the moment
AIDA, benefits, and only true claims
To remember. One reader, one offer, one action. Ask so what of every sentence. Start with her pain, in her words. Keep your voice steady, and fit the tone to the moment. And only true claims.

Why it matters
Four short formats do most selling

Descriptions replace you, the seller
Status and captions are your shop window

Most people see only your first line and the picture before deciding.
Online, she cannot touch the product, so your words must do it for her.
WhatsApp status and Instagram are the shop window for many Nigerian businesses.
And a clear call to action turns interest into an order.
Headlines
Chioma's laundry headline
Before
Best Laundry Services in Town
Vague, not urgent
Every laundry says this
After
Busy in Enugu?
Washed, ironed, delivered in 48 hours
Resumption week: drop off by Thursday
Test headlines with the 4 U's: useful, urgent, unique and ultra-specific. For example, Chioma runs a laundry in Enugu. Best Laundry Services in Town scores on none of them.
Her new line: Busy in Enugu? Your clothes washed, ironed and delivered in 48 hours. For the season: resumption week, drop off by Thursday, wear crisp uniforms on Monday.
Clear beats clever. Write ten headlines in ten minutes, then choose the best, never the first.
Product descriptions
The four-part description
No 'organic' or health claims you cannot prove.
Hook: the main benefit
Benefits, each with a feature as proof
Practical details: size, ingredients, price
Call to action: what to send
For example, Amaka sells whipped shea butter in Abuja. Her old description said: Organic shea butter. Very good for skin. Organic is a claim she cannot prove, and very good is vague.
Part one, the hook: Soft, whipped shea butter that melts into dry skin without leaving you oily.
Part two, benefits with proof: made with raw shea butter and coconut oil, so it absorbs quickly. Whipped for 20 minutes, so it spreads easily, even in harmattan.
Part three, details: a 250g jar, the real ingredients, how to store it, the price of 4,500 naira, and delivery in 1 to 2 days.
Part four, the action: Reply SHEA with your area to order.
Never claim a product cures or treats a disease unless it is approved for that. Food, drinks and cosmetics sold widely generally need NAFDAC registration.
Be specific
Vague words, specific words
Vague
Specific
5 litres, a week of family cooking
Same-day in Ikeja, order by noon
Words like quality, big and fast tell the buyer nothing she can check.

Replace them with details: double-stitched seams and a metal zip. 5 litres, enough for a week of family cooking. Same-day delivery in Ikeja if you order before 12 noon. Specific words sound like someone who has really used the product.
Tolu's five-status day
Morning: party this weekend?
Proof: fried fresh on the day
Details: what is in each pack, price
Customer message, with permission
Evening: 3 more orders, reply PACK
One idea per status. For example, Tolu sells small chops in Ibadan. Instead of one crowded flyer with 12 items, she posts a series. Morning: planning a party this weekend? 50 packs ready in 24 hours.
Then a video of puff-puff frying: fresh, not reheated.
Then what is in each pack, at about 2,000 naira this month.
Then a customer's thank-you message, shared with permission.
And in the evening: I can take 3 more weekend orders. Reply PACK with the date and number of guests. Together, the series follows Attention, Interest, Desire and Action.
Instagram
Caption checklist
First line works like a headline
Value: a tip or the product's story
Proof and details, with price
A handful of specific hashtags

Instagram cuts a caption off after the first line or two, so the first line must work like a headline. For example, Bisi sells adire in Abeokuta: Every piece was tied and dyed by hand, so no two wrappers are the same.
Then the story, details with price, one action, and specific hashtags like adire and Abeokuta, not general ones like love.
Calls to action
Make ordering one tap
Pay only into your business account. Never ask for PINs or OTPs.
One clear verb and one channel
The exact next step to send
Price and delivery cost shown first
Say how payment works
A wa.me link with a pre-filled message
Patronise us is not a call to action. Use a clear verb, like reply, book or order, and one channel, the one you answer fastest.
Give the exact next step: reply ORDER with your delivery area and I will send the total.
Remove friction. Show the price and the delivery cost before the call to action.
Say how payment works, and add reassurance, like your response time or exchange policy.

A WhatsApp click-to-chat link opens a chat with you in one tap. Grace in Abuja types wa.me, then her number with 234 instead of the first 0, and adds a message so the customer only presses send. She tests it on her own phone first.
Ask buyers to pay only into an account in your business or registered name, and never ask for card PINs, OTPs or passwords. Saying this in your copy reassures buyers who fear scams.

Why it matters
Longer copy for bigger jobs
Paid ads reach strangers
A sales page answers every question
Broadcasts feel like personal messages
You own your email list
A paid Facebook or Instagram ad reaches people who do not know you, so your words must work harder and faster.
A sales page explains an offer that needs more than a caption, like a class or a pre-order.
A WhatsApp broadcast arrives as a private message, so it should read like one.
And unlike followers, you own your email list.
Ads
PAS: Uche's generator ad
Talk about the situation, not the person.
Problem: name one she recognises
Agitate: its real cost, honestly
Solution: your offer, with proof
Action: one tap, one next step
PAS stands for Problem, Agitate, Solution. For example, Uche services generators in Owerri. Problem: does your generator start, run for a few minutes, then go off?
Agitate: you keep pulling the rope, food in the freezer starts to spoil, and you buy fuel for a machine that will not stay on. Factual, not frightening.
Solution: home servicing in Owerri, carburettor cleaning, plug and oil change, and a test run, from about 10,000 naira depending on size.
Action: tap Send WhatsApp message and tell us your generator brand and size.
Meta's ad standards do not allow copy that asks about someone's health, money or body. Are you broke? will be rejected. Does your generator keep going off? is about the generator, not the person.
Sales pages
Follow the reader's questions
Headline: the promise, and who it is for
Problem: show you understand her
Benefits, each with proof
Offer, price and honest limit
FAQ, then one clear button
For example, Funke runs baking classes in Lagos. Her headline: Bake soft bread and cakes you can sell, in 4 Saturdays.
The problem: you have watched many videos, but your cakes still sink, and you are not sure how to price what you bake.
Benefits with proof: bake with your own hands, take home recipes, and learn to cost a recipe. Plus real student comments, shared with permission.
The offer: a fee of 60,000 naira, ingredients included. Only 12 seats per class, so everyone gets hands-on time. That limit is true, so the urgency is honest.
Then the FAQ, taken straight from her chats: do I need an oven at home? Can I pay in two parts? Answer honestly, never dodge. Then one button: Reserve my seat.
Benefit bullets
One detail beats three adjectives
Weak
Strong
Bake 6 recipes yourself
Learn to cost a recipe for profit
8 years running a home bakery
Words like amazing and expert tell the buyer nothing.
Start each bullet with the result, and add one specific detail. Bake 6 recipes yourself, from bread to meat pie. And only write 8 years of experience if it is true.
Design for phones first: short paragraphs, small photos, and a button a thumb can reach.
WhatsApp broadcasts
Ifeoma's restock broadcast
Before
DEAR VALUED CUSTOMERS!!!
All kinds of lace, very cheap
Added without asking
After
Good morning. Wine lace is back
5 yards, about N38,000
14 pieces, 6 reserved
Reply WINE to reserve
A broadcast list sends one message privately to many contacts, but only people who saved your number receive it.
For example, Ifeoma sells fabric in Aba. She used to add every customer without asking, and shout in capital letters. Some blocked her.
Now she asks first: would you like new arrivals once a week? Reply YES to join, and STOP any time.
Her message is calm and specific: the wine Swiss lace is back, 5 yards for about 38,000 naira, 14 pieces with 6 reserved. Reply WINE to reserve one.
Stay safe and welcome
Three broadcast rules
Ask before adding anyone, and make leaving easy. It respects the Data Protection Act 2023.
One to two broadcasts a week often works better than daily. Mix offers with useful tips.
Tell your list your account number, and that you never ask for card PINs or OTPs.
Ask permission first. It keeps people from blocking you, and respects Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023.
Send one to two broadcasts a week, at a time customers are free, and mix offers with useful tips. If replies drop, you are sending too often.

Scammers sometimes copy a seller's name and photo. Tell your list which account number you use, that you never ask for card PINs or OTPs, and send payment details only after a customer confirms an order.
Email
Before you send an email
Real sender name people recognise
Short, specific, honest subject line
Preview text written, not left blank
One goal, one button, a P.S.
Only people who agreed; unsubscribe link

For example, Ruth launches office lunches in Abuja. Not Ruth's Kitchen Update, but: Hot office lunches for your team, delivered by 12:30. She writes the preview text, offers one goal, a free tasting day, and adds a P.S. with an honest limit.
Only email people who agreed, never buy lists, and always include an unsubscribe link.
Key points
Remember
PAS for felt problems, AIDA for desire
Describe situations, not people
Sales page follows the reader's questions
Broadcasts: permission, one point, one action
Email: one goal, consent, unsubscribe

To remember. Use PAS for felt problems and AIDA for desire. Describe situations, not people. Build sales pages in the order of the reader's questions. Ask permission before broadcasting. And give every email one goal.

Why it matters

People remember stories more easily than lists of features.

Using the words customers search with helps them find you on Google.
And testing shows what your customers actually prefer.
Storytelling
The customer is the hero. Never invent a story.
Action: one low-risk next step
For example, Esther tutors maths in Benin City, and a parent agreed to share his daughter's story. Before: in January, Osaro sat for an hour and finished two questions.
After: by the end of the term, she finished her homework before dinner and asked for extra fractions practice.
Bridge: two evenings a week, we went back to the basics she had missed, with objects and drawings for fractions, and small wins every session.
Action: we have 4 places left this term. Reply MATHS to hear how the free assessment works.
Specific, true details make it believable. A made-up customer story is a fake testimonial, so only use real stories, with permission.
Objections
Sade answers 'too expensive'
For example, Sade sells handmade leather sandals in Ibadan, and buyers say 'too expensive'.
Leather sandals, one pair
About per month, over two years
Lighter slip-on style
Naira prices are approximate.

An objection is a reason a buyer hesitates: trust, price, delivery or fit. For example, Sade's leather sandals. Many people reply, too expensive. Instead of arguing, she explains the value: full cow leather and a stitched sole, not glued.
The sandals cost about 25,000 naira a pair.
If a pair lasts two years of regular wear, that is about 1,050 naira a month. She only says this because her past customers report that kind of wear.
And for a lighter pocket, she offers her slip-on style at about 15,000 naira. She also confirms the size before payment, which removes the fit worry.
Some buyers will still say no, and that is fine.
Testimonials
Ethical proof only
Gifts or discounts disclosed
Private details hidden
Rare best result shown as normal

Yetunde told Sade she danced all night at a wedding, no pain. Sade asked: may I share your message with your first name only? She kept Yetunde's meaning, removed the unrelated line, and covered her phone number and photo.
Never write reviews yourself or present unusual results as typical. In Nigeria, the FCCPC enforces the law against misleading claims.
And only promise exchange or refund policies you can actually honour.
Google search
Bukola's page that nobody found
Check autocomplete for real phrases
Title: Small Chops Delivery in Ibadan
Description written like an ad
Headings that are customer questions
Write naturally; never keyword-stuff
For example, Bukola caters in Ibadan, and her page was titled Home. She typed her product and town into Google and saw phrases like small chops in Ibadan.
Her new title uses that phrase and her brand name.
Her meta description reads like an ad: fresh packs for parties and offices, fried on the day, order on WhatsApp.
Her subheadings are real questions: what is in each pack, and which areas do you deliver to?
Do not repeat the same phrase over and over. Google treats keyword stuffing as a bad practice. A free Google Business Profile also helps local buyers find you on Maps.

Good copy is rewritten. For example, Hauwa's zobo draft began: we wish to inform our esteemed customers. She cut the filler and added specifics: hibiscus, ginger and pineapple, 50cl bottles, about 700 naira each, delivered cold in Jos by 1pm. Reply ZOBO.
Her draft went from 52 words to 36, and says much more. Read your copy aloud, and rewrite wherever you stumble.
A/B testing
Hauwa tests two first lines
Change only one thing. One small test is a clue, not a law.
Test only the first line
A: price-led. B: taste-led
Same picture, price and time
Record views and replies
Keep the winner, test the next thing
An A/B test compares two versions that differ in only one thing. Hauwa tests only her first line.
Version A: Chilled zobo, 12 bottles for about 8,000 naira. Version B: Hibiscus, ginger and pineapple, served ice cold.
Everything else stays the same. She posts each at 10am on alternate days, for two weeks.
A got 21 replies from 410 views, about 5.1%. B got 9 replies from 395 views, about 2.3%.
So she keeps the price-led line, and next tests the call to action.
Measure replies and orders, not only likes. If results are close, treat it as a tie.
